paragraphs: “As God’s my witness, it’s involuntary! I never used to say it. I said ‘sir’ to nobody all my life, but the moment I sank into low water I started saying ‘sir.’ It’s the work of some higher power. I see you’re interested in the questions of the day. But how can I have roused your curiosity, when I live in surroundings where there’s no possibility of hospitality?”
“I’ve come—about that business.”
“What business?” the captain cut in impatiently.
“About your meeting with my brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Alyosha blurted out awkwardly.

“What meeting, sir? Surely not that meeting? Is it my ‘wisp of tow’ you mean, then?” He moved closer, so close that his knees actually knocked against Alyosha’s. His lips were pressed together oddly, thin as a thread.
“What wisp of tow?” Alyosha muttered.

“He’s come to complain about me, Father!” cried a voice Alyosha knew—the schoolboy’s voice—from behind the curtain. “I bit his finger just now.” The curtain was pulled back, and Alyosha saw his attacker lying on a little bed made up on the bench and a chair in the corner, under the ikons. The boy lay covered with his coat and an old quilted blanket. He was plainly unwell, and from his glittering eyes he had a fever. He looked at Alyosha without fear, as though he knew he was at home and couldn’t be touched.
“What! He bit your finger?” The captain jumped up from his chair. “Was it your finger he bit?”

“Yes. He was throwing stones with some other schoolboys. There were six of them against him alone. I went up to him, and he threw a stone at me, and then another at my head. I asked him what I’d done to him. Then he rushed at me and bit my finger badly. I don’t know why.”
“I’ll thrash him, sir, right now—this minute!” The captain sprang up from his seat.
“But I’m not complaining at all, I’m just telling you ... I don’t want him thrashed. Besides, he seems to be ill.”

“And do you suppose I would thrash him? That I’d take my Ilusha and thrash him in front of you, to satisfy you? Would you like it done at once, sir?” said the captain, suddenly turning on Alyosha as though he meant to attack him. “I’m sorry about your finger, sir. But instead of thrashing Ilusha, would you like me to chop off my own four fingers with this knife, right here before your eyes, to satisfy your just anger? I should think four fingers would be enough to quench your thirst for revenge. You won’t ask for the fifth as well?” He stopped short, his voice catching in his throat. Every feature of his face was twitching and working; he looked extremely defiant. He was in a kind of frenzy.

“I think I understand it all now,” said Alyosha, gently and sorrowfully, still keeping his seat. “So your boy is a good boy. He loves his father, and he attacked me because I’m the brother of the man who wronged you.... Now I understand,” he repeated thoughtfully. “My brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch regrets what he did, I know that. If it’s possible for him to come to you—or better still, to meet you in that same place—he’ll ask your forgiveness in front of everyone, if you wish it.”
“After pulling out my beard, you mean, he’ll ask my forgiveness? And he thinks that will make a satisfactory finish, does he?”
“Oh, no! On the contrary, he’ll do anything you like, and in any way you like.”
“So if I were to ask his highness to go down on his knees before me in that very tavern—‘The Metropolis’ it’s called—or in the marketplace, he would do it?”
“Yes, he would even go down on his knees.”

“You’ve pierced me to the heart, sir. You’ve moved me to tears and pierced me to the heart! I’m only too aware of your brother’s generosity. Allow me to introduce my family: my two daughters and my son—my litter. If I die, who will look after them? And while I live, who but they will care for a wretch like me? That’s a great thing the Lord has arranged for every man of my sort, sir. For there must be someone who can love even a man like me.”
“Ah, that’s perfectly true!” exclaimed Alyosha.
“Oh, stop playing the fool! Some idiot walks in, and you make us look ridiculous!” cried the girl by the window, suddenly turning to her father with a scornful, contemptuous look.
“Wait a little, Varvara!” cried her father, speaking sharply but looking at her quite approvingly. “That’s her character,” he said, turning to Alyosha again.
“And in all nature there was naught That could find favor in his eyes—

or rather, in the feminine: that could find favor in her eyes. But now let me present you to my wife, Arina Petrovna. She’s crippled, she’s forty-three; she can move, but very little. She’s of humble origin. Arina Petrovna, compose your face. This is Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov. Get up, Alexey Fyodorovitch.” He took him by the hand and, with surprising strength, pulled him to his feet. “You must stand to be introduced to a lady. It’s not the Karamazov, mamma, who ... h’m ... et cetera, but his brother, radiant with modest virtues. Come, Arina Petrovna, come, mamma, first your hand to be kissed.”

And he kissed his wife’s hand respectfully, even tenderly. The girl at the window turned her back on the scene in disgust. An expression of extraordinary warmth came over the haughty, questioning face of the woman.
“Good morning! Sit down, Mr. Tchernomazov,” she said.
“Karamazov, mamma, Karamazov. We’re of humble origin,” he whispered again.

“Well, Karamazov, or whatever it is, but I always think of Tchernomazov.... Sit down. Why did he pull you up? He calls me crippled, but I’m not. It’s only that my legs are swollen like barrels, and I myself am shriveled up. I used to be so fat, but now it’s as if I’d swallowed a needle.”
“We’re of humble origin,” the captain muttered again.
“Oh, Father, Father!” said the hunchback girl, who had been silent on her chair until then, and she hid her eyes in her handkerchief.
“Buffoon!” blurted out the girl at the window.

“Have you heard our news?” said the mother, pointing at her daughters. “It’s like clouds coming over; the clouds pass and we have music again. When we were with the army, we used to have a lot of guests like this. I don’t mean to compare anyone; everyone to their own taste. The deacon’s wife used to come then and say, ‘Alexandr Alexandrovitch is a man of the noblest heart, but Nastasya Petrovna,’ she’d say, ‘is of the brood of hell.’ ‘Well,’ I said, ‘that’s a matter of taste. But you’re a little spitfire.’ ‘And you need keeping in your place,’ says she. ‘You black sword,’ said I, ‘who asked you to teach me?’ ‘But my breath,’ says she, ‘is clean, and yours is foul.’ ‘Go and ask all the officers whether my breath is foul.’ And ever since then I’ve had it on my mind. Not long ago I was sitting here just as I am now, when I saw that very general come in, the one who came here at Easter, and I asked him: ‘Your Excellency,’ said I, ‘can a lady’s breath be unpleasant?’ ‘Yes,’ he answered; ‘you ought to open a window-pane or open the door, for the air isn’t fresh in here.’ And they all go on like that! And what is my breath to them? The dead smell worse still! ‘I won’t spoil the air,’ said I, ‘I’ll order some slippers and go away.’ My darlings, don’t blame your own mother! Nikolay Ilyitch, how is it I can’t please you? There’s only Ilusha who comes home from school and loves me. Yesterday he brought me an apple. Forgive your own mother—forgive a poor lonely creature! Why has my breath become unpleasant to you?”
And the poor mad woman burst into sobs, and tears streamed down her cheeks. The captain rushed over to her.

“Mamma, mamma, my dear, stop it! You’re not lonely. Everyone loves you, everyone adores you.” He began kissing both her hands again and tenderly stroking her face; then he took the dinner napkin and began wiping away her tears. Alyosha thought he had tears in his own eyes too. “There, you see, you hear?” he said, turning on Alyosha with a kind of fury and pointing at the poor imbecile.
“I see and hear,” muttered Alyosha.
“Father, Father, how can you—with him! Leave him alone!” cried the boy, sitting up in his bed and staring at his father with glowing eyes.
“Stop fooling around! Stop showing off your silly antics that never lead to anything!” shouted Varvara, stamping her foot in a passion.

“Your anger is quite just this time, Varvara, and I’ll hurry to satisfy you. Come, put on your cap, Alexey Fyodorovitch, and I’ll put on mine. We’ll go out. I have something to say to you in earnest, but not within these walls. This girl sitting here is my daughter Nina; I forgot to introduce her to you. She is a heavenly angel incarnate ... who has flown down to us mortals,... if you can understand.”
“Look at him shaking all over, as if he were in convulsions!” Varvara went on indignantly.

“And she there, stamping her foot at me and calling me a fool just now, she’s a heavenly angel incarnate too, and she has good reason to call me that. Come along, Alexey Fyodorovitch, we must make an end of this.”
And, snatching Alyosha’s hand, he drew him out of the room and into the street.
